More specifically, it amends Regulations (EC) No 561/2006, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2019/2144, and (EU) 2024/1257, with the objective of reducing unnecessary regulatory complexity, eliminating overlaps, and improving consistency across EU vehicle legislation. It seeks to make type-approval and compliance procedures more efficient for manufacturers and authorities, better reflecting technological progress and current market conditions.
Moreover, as part of this simplification effort, the proposal repeals Council Directive 70/157/EEC and Regulation (EU) No 540/2014, which contain outdated or redundant provisions, notably in the area of vehicle noise and technical standards. Their repeal contributes to greater legal clarity and consolidation of applicable rules within the updated regulatory framework.
The proposed Regulation concerns the following:
Removing regulatory obstacles for the uptake of electric light commercial vehicles
Electric light commercial vehicles are heavier as the result of the weight of their battery. An amendment allows Member States to exempt N2 e-vans - with a maximum authorised mass exceeding 3.5 tonnes but not exceeding 4.25 tonnes - engaged exclusively in domestic transport, from the obligation to install smart tachographs, in order to put them on equal footing with their fossil fuel equivalent, N1 diesel vans.
The main expected impact for the proposed measure is a reduced cost for companies, in particular SMEs that are the primary users/buyers of such vans, that will no longer have to install smart tachographs for the given type of e-van. In addition, the removal of the tachograph will also determine a reduction of administrative burden/costs for the companies/drivers who will no longer have to download tachograph data (2 to 4 hours a month). Moreover, levelling the playing field between N1 diesel vans and N2 e-vans through reduced prices for the latter will help stimulate the uptake of such e-vans.
In order to clarify the legal framework applicable to the specific case of motorhomes with a maximum authorized mass exceeding 7.5 tonnes used for private purposes, a second proposed amendment consists of allowing Member States to exempt motorhomes from the rules relating to driving times and rest periods, as well as the tachograph.
Accelerating the uptake of small affordable electric vehicles
The proposal establishes the legal basis for a new ‘small EV’ category , covering pure electric passenger cars below a defined length threshold. There is currently a lack of small affordable electric vehicles on the European market. In September 2025, the Commission President announced a small affordable car initiative aimed to incentivise the market for small electric vehicles. This will require targeted regulatory measures. The Commission will endeavour to freeze new requirements for 10 years and propose targeted incentives in the CO2 vehicle emission standards for small electric vehicles. The initiative may also lead to fiscal (such as subsidy schemes) and non-fiscal incentives (such as reserved parking space), compatible with State aid rules, where applicable. For this purpose, it is necessary to add a definition of a small electric car in motor vehicle legislation that can be used for targeted measures in EU legislation and by Member States. This would bring simplification for businesses, strengthen the business case to build small affordable electric cars profitably in Europe and reduce the price for consumers.
Simplifying the type-approval framework
With the increasing speed of innovation in the industry, in particular trends on automated driving and software updates, it is appropriate to assess the simplification potential in the EU type-approval framework for motor vehicles. Regulatory complexity can be a constraint for EU manufacturers in global competition with manufacturers from other jurisdictions. The proposal aligns EU type-approval requirements more closely with international standards, while expanding the Commission’s powers to adopt delegated acts on technical requirements for EVs.
The changes also aim to refer to ‘vehicle categories’ rather than ‘vehicle types’ for type approval of Euro 7 engines.
Reducing the adjustment costs related to Euro 7 emission tests
Annex V of the Euro 7 Regulation requires for the type-approval of heavy-duty vehicle engines tests per vehicle type. This requirement will introduce unnecessary administrative and regulatory burden by multiplying tests without providing additional environmental benefits. Therefore, the proposal streamlines emissions testing under the Euro 7 regime. It also provides for the development of on-board fuel consumption monitoring (OBFCM) devices and on-board monitoring (OBM) systems, as well as common methods for data processing.
Based on available information, it is expected that the amendments will result in significant annual savings of EUR 706 million for industry, including SMEs, citizens and public administrations.

Source: OEIL procedure file 2025/0422(COD)
ai_summary:
This proposal is meant to simplify and update the EU's rules for motor vehicles, cutting red tape and removing overlaps while keeping road safety, environmental protection and market oversight in place. It amends several existing EU vehicle laws and repeals two older ones that contain outdated or duplicate rules, mainly on vehicle noise and technical standards. The European Parliament will decide on it together with the Council, on an equal footing.

The proposal is part of a wider package called the Automotive Omnibus, which aims to remove rules that make it harder for electric vehicles to compete, especially light commercial vehicles and small passenger cars. The EU's car industry is a major part of the economy, linked to about 10.6 million direct jobs, and industry representatives say the number of rules manufacturers must meet by 2030 is driving research and development costs up, in some cases by as much as 25%.

For electric light commercial vehicles, the proposal lets Member States exempt certain electric vans, those above 3.5 tonnes but not above 4.25 tonnes that are used only for domestic transport, from having to install smart tachographs. This is meant to put them on equal footing with comparable diesel vans, lowering costs for businesses, especially small ones, and cutting the time spent downloading tachograph data. It also lets Member States exempt private motorhomes over 7.5 tonnes from driving-time rules, rest-period rules and the tachograph requirement.

The proposal also creates a legal definition of a "small EV," a pure electric passenger car below a set length threshold, so that targeted measures can be applied to such cars. The aim is to encourage affordable small electric cars, which are currently scarce on the European market. Possible support includes incentives in CO2 standards, subsidies and non-financial benefits such as reserved parking, and the Commission would aim to freeze new requirements for these cars for 10 years.

Finally, the proposal simplifies the EU type-approval system, bringing it closer to international standards and widening the Commission's power to set technical requirements for electric vehicles. It also streamlines Euro 7 emissions testing for heavy-duty engines, so that tests are not repeated for every vehicle type without extra environmental benefit, and supports new on-board fuel consumption and monitoring systems. The proposal is expected to save industry, citizens and public administrations EUR 706 million a year.

Official summary (Legislative Observatory, Legislative proposal published):
PURPOSE: to accelerate the uptake of zero- and low-emission vehicles in corporate fleets, while fostering the competitiveness of the Union’s automotive sector.

PROPOSED ACT: Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council.

ROLE OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT: the European Parliament decides in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure and on an equal footing with the Council.

BACKGROUND: corporate vehicles have a significant potential to accelerate the uptake of zero-emission vehicles (ZEV), due to their high share in new vehicle registrations (around 60% for new registration of cars and around 90% for new registration of vans) and their specific characteristics in terms of vehicle operations.
Due to the high share of corporate vehicles in new vehicle registrations, and their specific characteristics in terms of vehicle operations, measures targeting corporate vehicles have significant potential to accelerate the uptake of zero- and low-emission vehicles and the reduction of road transport emissions in the Union. However, that potential is currently underexploited. Corporate vehicles are responsible for a comparatively higher share of emissions compared to private vehicles, due to their generally higher yearly mileage, as is the case for example for some corporate fleets such as taxi and ride-hailing. A higher share of zero- and low-emission vehicles in those high-mileage fleets would result in high real-world fuel savings and emission reductions compared to current trends.

CONTENT: the proposed regulation establishes a framework for increasing the uptake of zero-and low-emission vehicles within the Union. It sets targets for the share of zero- and low emission vehicles in new corporate cars and vans registered by large undertakings in each Member State. This regulation does not prevent any Member State from setting more ambitious targets.
National targets
In view of the need to stimulate the market for zero- and low-emission vehicles while also supporting the further deployment of alternative fuels and leaving appropriate flexibility to Member States and market actors, the Commission has decided to set national targets. These targets will encourage Member States to put in place measures to incentivise the use of corporate zero- and low-emission vehicles by large companies . The design of the measures is at the discretion of each Member State . The resulting increase in the share of new zero- and low-emission vehicles in corporate fleets can help reduce road transport emissions faster, while increasing the availability of zero- and low- emission vehicles for citizens and businesses that rely on second-hand vehicles. These national targets are set at different levels of ambition for cars and vans in order to reflect the different levels of technology and market development, as well as the differences in targets for the respective vehicle categories under the CO2 emission performance standards. They are also differentiated between Member States in order to take account of the specific situation and characteristics of different Member States, in relation to their economy’s ability to address the higher initial capital costs of ZEV.
In respect the principle of technological neutrality, and to leave sufficient flexibility to the Member States, the proposal should set national targets that can be met through the combined share of zero- and low-emission vehicles.
The methodology to calculate those shares for the purpose of demonstrating compliance with the While the initiative introduces targets for Member States in the form of the share of new zero- and low-emission vehicles for large companies, the additional administrative burden for public authorities is kept to a minimum. The proposal builds on existing vehicle datasets and modalities that Member States already operate for vehicle registration and statistics, including business and fiscal statistics. While all Member States already have the necessary systems in place to identify new registrations of corporate vehicles, for distinguishing vehicle registered by SMEs or large companies in place, one-off administrative costs are expected.
SMEs are excluded from the scope of the proposal, which only targets new corporate vehicles registered by large companies (companies with at least 250 employees and EUR 50 million turnover), irrespective of their economic field of activity.
‘Made in the EU’
Since the transition towards zero-emission vehicles in corporate fleets may be subject to public financial support in Member States, there is a potential for using public support to help strengthen domestic value chains in the automotive sector.
Cars and vans ‘made in the European Union’ can contribute to the creation of a stable lead market for European suppliers, enhancing the competitiveness of Union industry, maintaining its workforce and helping attract new investments in Union production capacity in those sectors. To qualify for public financial support, vehicles will in the future have to be zero- or low-emission and manufactured in the EU. The Commission will rely on delegated acts to set up a methodology for determining the criteria for a car or van to be considered ‘made in EU’.

Source: OEIL procedure file 2025/0421(COD)
ai_summary:
This proposed EU regulation aims to speed up the switch to zero- and low-emission vehicles in company fleets, while helping the EU's car industry stay competitive. The European Parliament and the Council would decide on it together, as equal partners.

The reasoning is that company vehicles are a large share of new registrations, about 60% of new cars and about 90% of new vans. They are also driven more miles per year than private cars, so they produce a disproportionate share of emissions. Shifting these high-mileage fleets to cleaner vehicles could bring real fuel savings and emission cuts sooner than current trends would.

To do this, the regulation sets national targets for the share of zero- and low-emission cars and vans that large companies register in each Member State. Each country decides for itself which measures to use to encourage this, and no country is prevented from setting more ambitious targets. The targets differ between cars and vans and between countries, reflecting differences in technology, market development, and each country's economic ability to cover the higher upfront cost of these vehicles. Countries can meet their targets using the combined share of zero- and low-emission vehicles, so they are not tied to one technology.

The regulation only covers large companies, defined as those with at least 250 employees and EUR 50 million in turnover. Small and medium-sized enterprises are excluded. The extra paperwork for public authorities should be small, since existing vehicle registration and statistics systems can mostly be used, though some one-off costs are expected to tell large and small company registrations apart.

The regulation also links public money to European manufacturing. In future, vehicles would have to be both zero- or low-emission and made in the EU to qualify for public financial support tied to this shift. The Commission will set the detailed rules for what counts as "made in the EU" later, through delegated acts. The aim is to build a stable home market for European suppliers, protect jobs, and attract investment in EU vehicle production.

2025/0255(COD) | Justice programme 2028-2034
Rapporteur: Tineke Strik (Greens/EFA) | Lead committee: JURI

📅 13 November 2026 | 🧭 Negotiating mandate for trilogue talks
What's next: Trilogue talks with the Council can begin once the Council side has its own mandate. Closed-door rounds follow; timing is not published.

Official summary (Legislative Observatory, Legislative proposal published):
PURPOSE: to establish the Justice programme for the period 2028-2034 and to repeal Regulation (EU) 2021/693.

PROPOSED ACT: Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council.

ROLE OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT: the European Parliament decides in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure and on an equal footing with the Council.

BACKGROUND: on 16 July 2025, the European Commission unveiled its proposal for the next multiannual financial framework (MFF) 2028-2034 , a EUR 2 trillion budget designed to strengthen Europe's sovereignty, competitiveness, and resilience. This new MFF will significantly enhance the EU's capacity to deliver on core policies while addressing new and emerging priorities.
Based on the positive experience from the implementation of the previous Justice programmes, the Commission proposes to continue the implementation of the new programme, with direct management by the Commission and a limited number of initiatives implemented under indirect management (for example by international organisations and public law bodies) in accordance with the Financial Regulation ( Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2024/2509 ).
This proposal sets out the legal basis for the Justice programme for the period 2028-2034.

CONTENT: the proposed regulation establishes the Justice Programme and lays down the objectives of the programme, its budget for the period 2028-2034, the forms of Union funding and the rules for providing such funding.
Objectives
The general objective of the proposed 2028-2034 Justice programme is to contribute to the further development of an efficient, inclusive, resilient and digitalised Union area of justice , based on the rule of law, mutual recognition and mutual trust . By achieving this objective, the programme will also strengthen democracy and the protection of fundamental rights and contribute to growth and competitiveness.
The general objective will be achieved through three specific objectives :
- to facilitate and support judicial cooperation in civil and criminal matters , and to promote the rule of law, in particular the independence, quality and efficiency of justice systems, including through improving the effective cross-border recognition and enforcement of judicial decisions;
- to promote and support training of the judiciary and judicial staff , with a view to promoting the rule of law, fundamental rights and democracy, fostering a common legal and judicial culture, ensuring the consistent and effective implementation of the relevant Union legal instruments and providing a supportive environment for the digitalisation of judicial cooperation and justice systems;
- to facilitate and support effective and non-discriminatory access to justice for all and effective remedy , including by digital means, by promoting efficient civil and criminal procedures and by promoting and supporting the rights of all victims of crime and the procedural rights of suspects and accused persons in criminal proceedings, as well as of requested persons in European Arrest Warrant proceedings.
The programme will provide for synergies between its different specific objectives to effectively support the policy areas these objectives cover and increase their potential to reach its target groups. To be effective, the programme should take into account the specific nature of the different policies, their different target groups and their particular needs through tailor-made approaches.
In implementing the proposed regulation, the Commission will set the funding priorities in the respective policy areas each year. The regulation’s structure allows for flexibility and for quick adjustments to be made based on policy needs and new policy and technological developments.
Budgetary implications
A financial envelope of EUR 798 million (current prices) is included under this new multiannual financial framework covering the period 1 January 2028 to 31 December 2034 for the Justice Programme.

Source: OEIL procedure file 2025/0255(COD)

ai_summary:
This proposal sets out the legal basis for a new EU Justice Programme covering 2028 to 2034, and it would replace an earlier regulation from 2021. The European Parliament and the Council would decide on it together, as equal partners. The European Commission would run most of the programme directly, with a small number of initiatives carried out by other bodies such as international organisations and public law bodies.

The programme's overall aim is to help build a fair, efficient, resilient and increasingly digital area of justice across the EU, based on the rule of law and on countries trusting and recognising each other's legal decisions. This is also meant to support democracy, protect fundamental rights, and contribute to economic growth and competitiveness.

The programme pursues three main goals. The first is to support cooperation between countries in civil and criminal cases, promote the rule of law, and make justice systems more independent, high-quality and efficient, including by making it easier to recognise and enforce court decisions across borders. The second is to train judges and court staff, so that EU law is applied consistently, a shared legal culture develops, and the move to digital justice is supported. The third is to make sure everyone can access justice on equal, non-discriminatory terms and obtain an effective remedy, including online, while protecting the rights of crime victims and of suspects and accused people, including people subject to European Arrest Warrant proceedings.

The programme is designed so that these goals support one another and reach their intended groups through approaches suited to each area. Each year the Commission will decide the funding priorities, and the rules are meant to be flexible enough to adapt quickly to changing policy needs and new technology.

A total of EUR 798 million (in current prices) is set aside for the Justice Programme for the whole 2028 to 2034 period.

The European Parliament has approved, with 495 votes in favour, 57 against and 45 abstentions, its position on a proposed EU directive that would create a single code for medicines for human use. The directive would replace two existing directives, 2001/83/EC and 2009/35/EC.

The directive would cover medicines for people that are meant to be sold in EU member countries. When it is unclear whether a substance or product counts as a medicine, the national authority, or the European Medicines Agency for centrally approved products, would consult other relevant advisory bodies before deciding.

Advanced therapy medicines made under hospital exemption would have to follow good pharmacy preparation practices adapted to hospital work, which must still be equivalent to standard good manufacturing practice and traceability rules. This includes site inspections, traceability and safety monitoring plans, and review of the preclinical and clinical data. Hospitals would have to report patient follow-up data at least once a year to their national authority, and the Agency would keep a public database of this data and of approvals, suspensions and withdrawals, leaving out personal and confidential commercial information.

Companies applying for approval should not test on animals where scientifically satisfactory non-animal methods exist. Where such methods do not exist, any animal studies used must follow the principles of replacement, reduction and refinement.

Antibiotics and other antimicrobials should, wherever possible, be packaged in amounts matching the length of treatment, and where that is not possible, in pack sizes matching the usual dose and duration. Member States should encourage unit-dose pre-cut blisters in hospitals and, gradually, in pharmacies. Medicines with a known risk of antimicrobial resistance, or containing substances that are persistent, bioaccumulative and toxic or similarly harmful to the environment, would need a medical prescription. Antibiotic prescriptions would be limited to the amount and duration needed, and a justification would be required where no diagnostic test was carried out. Pharmacists and other health professionals would advise on the prudent use and correct disposal of antibiotics, and Member States would set up disposal systems and inform the public about them.

To improve access and reduce inequalities, marketing authorisation holders would have to apply for pricing and reimbursement in a Member State when requested. The application must be submitted within 12 months of that request, or within 24 months for small and medium-sized enterprises.

Package leaflets would be available electronically and on paper, except where a Member State chooses electronic-only information, and must be easy to read and understand. The Commission would assess online pharmaceutical advertising and promotion and set specific rules for it, and in emergencies such as the COVID-19 pandemic, healthcare professionals must still be able to give clear, impartial information. Member States would record all suspected adverse reactions reported to them and, where possible, tell those who reported them about safety decisions. Reports of reactions caused by incorrect administration or dispensing would go into the Eudravigilance database and into periodic safety reports.

This measure sets out EU-wide rules for approving, monitoring and tracking the safety of medicines for people, and for handling medicine shortages. It also sets out how the European Medicines Agency is run. The European Parliament adopted it by 488 votes to 67, with 34 abstentions, and it replaces three earlier regulations.

The rules cover three main areas: how medicines are authorised and supervised across the EU, how shortages and critical shortages are monitored and managed to keep supplies secure, and how the Agency itself is governed. For medicines containing genetically modified organisms, the environmental risk assessment must look at risks to the environment, animals and human health throughout the product's life, including production, and must describe how those risks would be reduced.

To encourage new antibiotics and other antimicrobials, which address growing resistance to existing treatments, the measure allows milestone payments for research progress before approval, along with a voluntary joint procurement scheme that pays for access separately from the amount sold. A developer may also receive a transferable data exclusivity voucher, which adds up to 12 months of data protection to one medicine. The length depends on how the pathogen is ranked: 12 months for "critical," 9 months for "high" and 6 months for "medium." A voucher can be used only once, only for one centrally authorised medicine, and only within that medicine's first four years of data protection. The Commission must report on the results within five years.

Other provisions require the Agency to keep scientific advice separate from later evaluation of the same product, with at least one of two assessors having taken no part in earlier advice. Orphan drugs for rare diseases can receive up to 11 years of market exclusivity if they address a high unmet medical need, and the Commission must propose a Union framework for rare diseases within 24 months. A public European medicines web-portal will provide information on approved medicines, and companies must give at least six months' notice before temporarily stopping supply in a Member State. The Agency will monitor shortages, and when critical shortages arise, national authorities and the Agency must coordinate to inform patients and professionals and to manage the situation.

The European Parliament has approved a proposed law on payment services across the EU's internal market, passing it by 511 votes to 22, with 75 abstentions. The law sets common rules for payment services and electronic money services, covering how clearly prices and terms must be shown and what rights and duties users and providers have.

Under the Parliament's position, anyone offering currency conversion to a payer at an ATM, at a shop, or through the payee must disclose all charges and the exchange rate before the payer approves the payment. A payee who adds a charge or offers a discount for a particular payment method must tell the payer before the payment starts. Companies providing cash withdrawals must clearly show any charges, including the exchange rate and any markup over the central bank's latest rate, both when the withdrawal begins and when the cash is handed over. Low-value payments, up to EUR 50 per transaction or with a spending limit of EUR 250, are exempt from some of these information requirements.

The law also sets rules for ATMs and for bank accounts. ATM operators that are authorised in the EU must show any fixed fee in money terms when the card is inserted or tapped, whichever card is used. Payees may offer payers discounts or encourage a particular payment method. A bank may refuse or close a payment account for a payment institution only on objective, non-discriminatory and proportionate grounds, and closure generally takes effect after at least four months' notice, unless it is due to fraud or illegal activity. People paying within the EU do not have to specify which member state the other party's account is in, as long as the account can be reached.

On security, users and their providers can agree fair and proportionate spending limits on a payment instrument. Providers must block an instrument when there are objectively justified security risks or suspicion of fraud. If a provider does not block it despite reasonable grounds to suspect fraud, the payer bears no financial consequences, unless the payer acted fraudulently. Providers must also offer a communication channel for reporting fraud, requesting unblocking, getting advice on suspected scams, and raising problems with payments.

If a provider suspects the payer of fraud, it must within 14 business days either refund an unauthorised payment or, after further investigation, show that the payer committed fraud. Electronic communications providers must also warn customers when new online scams appear, paying particular attention to vulnerable groups, and explain how to spot and avoid fraud. Finally, manufacturers of mobile devices and communications providers may take strictly necessary and proportionate measures to protect the hardware and software integrity when enabling interoperability, provided they justify those measures.

The European Parliament has approved a new directive on payment services and electronic money services in the EU's internal market. The vote was 484 in favour, 8 against, with 118 abstentions. The directive would replace two earlier directives (2015/2366/EU and 2009/110/EC) and makes some changes to Directive 98/26/EC.

The rules cover who may offer payment and electronic money services in the EU and how those businesses are supervised. A company that wants to offer these services must get authorisation from the authorities in its home Member State. Its application has to include a plan of the services it intends to offer, proof that it holds the required starting capital, and a description of how it protects customers' money. It must also explain how it manages the business and controls its risks, how it handles security incidents and customer complaints, how it protects sensitive payment data, and how it would keep operating in an emergency. The company must also name its directors and major shareholders, show that they are suitable, and provide a plan for winding up the business if it fails. It must additionally describe its audit arrangements and how it protects users and keeps its services reliable.

Payment institutions must hold starting capital of at least EUR 25,000, EUR 50,000 or EUR 150,000, depending on the services they provide. Their own funds may not fall below that starting capital or the other required amount. Authorisation is granted if the applicant is a legal person established in a Member State and has the required capital. Authorities must tell applicants within two months of receiving an application whether it has been approved, and must give reasons if it is refused.

An authorisation is valid throughout the EU. The home authority can withdraw it only if the firm has not used it within twelve months of obtaining it, or has not provided any of the authorised services for more than six consecutive months. Member States must keep public registers of payment institutions, and the European Banking Authority (EBA) must run a central electronic register.

Firms that outsource operational tasks must tell their home authorities. They may not outsource important operational functions, including ICT systems, in a way that weakens their internal controls or prevents regulators from monitoring their compliance. Each Member State must name the authorities responsible for authorising and supervising payment institutions. These may be public authorities or bodies recognised by national law, including national central banks. The directive also sets out rules for firms that want to operate in other Member States, whether by setting up there or by providing services across borders, and includes transitional provisions.

This proposal would update the EU's rules on consular protection, which is the help that embassies and consulates give to citizens abroad. The aim is to make sure EU citizens who have no consulate or embassy from their own country in a foreign country can still get help, especially during crises. The idea is driven by recent emergencies such as the COVID-19 pandemic, the situation in Afghanistan, Russia's war against Ukraine, the conflict in Sudan, and repatriations from Israel and Gaza.

The proposal changes when a citizen counts as "unrepresented," meaning their home country has no embassy or consulate effectively able to help them. It sets out criteria for deciding this, which are meant to be flexible and to take local conditions into account, such as how easy it is to travel or how safe the country is. An honorary consul from the citizen's home country can only be counted as providing help if the help requested falls within that consul's responsibilities, so citizens are not turned away by a consul who cannot assist them.

The rules are also expanded to cover evacuation, meaning moving people from a dangerous area to a safe place that does not have to be in an EU country, as well as bringing citizens back to EU territory. Member States may work with security and military personnel, honorary consuls, international organisations, and third-country diplomatic authorities when coordinating help. Countries may also offer citizens the option to register their travel or residence in a foreign country, so that authorities have better information on how many citizens are present and where, and can contact them during a crisis.

On costs, the unrepresented citizen would mainly be expected to repay the cost of the help they receive, either when they ask for it or later. Only if that does not happen would the helping country seek repayment from the citizen's home country. Countries that help citizens who do have representation in a crisis may also seek repayment, since it can be hard to tell the two groups apart in emergencies. Finally, the proposal puts into practice the right to an effective legal remedy in the context of consular protection.

This measure updates EU rules on what airlines owe passengers when flights are denied boarding, cancelled, or badly delayed. The European Parliament approved it by 646 votes to 12, with 3 abstentions.

Passengers keep the right to a refund or a new route when a flight is cancelled. They can still claim compensation for delays of more than three hours, for cancellations announced less than 14 days ahead, or when they are denied boarding. Compensation amounts depend on flight distance: EUR 250 for journeys up to 1,500 km, EUR 400 for intra-EU journeys over 1,500 km and other journeys between 1,500 km and 3,500 km, and EUR 600 for all other longer journeys. Airlines may cut compensation by 50% on their longest journeys if passengers are re-routed to their final destination after a disruption, or if the arrival delay is no more than four hours. If a plane lands at a different airport, the airline must arrange transport to the original airport, and passengers arriving more than three hours late there are entitled to compensation.

Airlines can avoid paying compensation when a disruption is caused by circumstances beyond their control. The rules now include a non-exhaustive list of such circumstances, such as natural disasters, war, bad weather, unruly passengers, and strikes by airport staff, air navigation providers, or ground handlers. Any such circumstance must be directly linked to the flight, and the airline must have taken all reasonable measures to avoid the disruption. Airlines must tell passengers which circumstance they are relying on when they refuse compensation.

After a disruption, airlines must digitally inform each passenger of their possible right to compensation and how to claim it, within four days of the end of their journey. Claims must be made within nine months of the departure date on the ticket. Within thirty days of a claim, the airline must either pay or explain in writing why it will not, and provide information on how to complain. Vouchers are voluntary, can be worth more than the amount owed, and any balance left when they expire must be refunded to the passenger's bank account.

Passengers gain several rights: they can take the return leg of a return ticket without paying extra even if they skipped the outbound flight; they can bring one personal item, such as a small bag or backpack, free of charge; airline fare listings must include a piece of hand luggage in the displayed price; and they can bring musical instruments on board, including in a seat where needed. Passengers can choose a digital or paper boarding pass for free, and airlines cannot require an account or app to access one. Name typos can be corrected for free if spotted at least 48 hours before travel and cannot be used as grounds for denying boarding.

Passengers with disabilities or reduced mobility, and unaccompanied minors, are entitled to compensation and assistance if they face delays or miss connections because requested help was not provided. People with disabilities or reduced mobility also get clearer compensation and replacement for damaged equipment. Airlines must let children under 14 sit next to their parents free of charge, and children in strollers must be given priority boarding.

A "Union Air Passenger Rights Label" will show passengers quickly whether this regulation applies to a journey, making it easier to compare ticket offers. It will appear only on journeys operated by EU carriers, which must apply the regulation on flights departing from or arriving in the EU.

summary:
PURPOSE: to establish an updated and improved legal framework for the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA).
PROPOSED ACT: Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council.
ROLE OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT: the European Parliament decides in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure and on an equal footing with the Council.
BACKGROUND: the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) was established in 2007 by Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 under the REACH Regulation to handle technical, scientific, and administrative tasks related to EU chemicals laws. Its role has since expanded to cover areas like biocides, classification and labelling, and drinking water. This has greatly increased ECHA's workload, with some scientific committees expected to double their opinions in coming years.
The proposed regulation contributes and facilitates the achievement of the objectives of the ‘One Substance, One Assessment’ approach based on a more transparent, coherent, predictable and simpler chemical safety assessment processes across different pieces of legislation.
Against this background, the Agency should be governed by a single Regulation in order to cover in one act the Agency’s extended tasks and involvement in the implementation of several pieces of legislation and to ensure its efficient and sustainable governance, taking into account the principles of the Common Approach. This Regulation should therefore replace the provisions of Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006.
This proposal is part of the sixth simplification omnibus to reduce compliance costs and administrative burden for the chemical industry while ensuring strong protection of human health and the environment.
CONTENT: the Commission proposal aims to strengthen the governance of the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) and increase the sustainability of its financing model. In addition, it will:
- provide it with updated and improved legal framework which would allow it to operate effectively and efficiently and also onboard new tasks seamlessly;
- abolish the requirement for the segregation of the different budget strands of the Agency (Chemicals - REACH/CLP, Biocides, Environmental directives) and merge them in one entity;
- positively impact ECHA’s daily management and allow for more flexibility in the use of the resources and streamline the financing of the Agency.
Structure and content of the proposal
Moreover, the proposal introduces a number of new provisions on the Agency that were not previously featured under REACH. These are as follows:
Objectives and tasks of ECHA
The Agency’s objectives and extended scope of tasks, stemming from different pieces of other EU legislation is reflected in the corresponding provisions of this proposal. The other EU legislation assigning tasks is reflected in Annex I of this proposal to ensure that the Agency’s responsibilities under other EU legislation are coherently and transparently reflected in this Regulation.
Organisational structure of ECHA
The current organisational structure of the Agency, including all bodies of the Agency established under REACH and Biocidal Products Regulation, is laid down in this proposal to provide a coherent overview of the Agency’s structure, which has expanded, together with its tasks, since the adoption of REACH. The Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety is listed as a stand-alone scientific committee among ECHA committees and bodies. The rules on the governance of the Agency’s committees are moved to this proposal, while the provisions on the specific tasks of the committees remain in REACH and BPR and are referred to in this proposal.
The role of the Executive Director
Compared to the provisions in REACH, the rules on the appointment of the Executive Director in this proposal better specify their employment and provide for the evaluation of their performance and accountability. The tasks of the Executive Director laid down in this proposal include, in addition to the existing tasks, drafting the Agency’s financial rules and clarifying the Executive Director’s role in coordinating between the different committees within the Agency in case of divergence between their scientific opinions.
Financial provisions
These include the rules on the single programming document of the Agency, which includes the three-year planning, the work programme of the following year and reporting requirements. The changes in the financial provisions result from the implementation of the Common Approach and the currently applicable financial rules for EU decentralised agencies. The changes introduced to the budget procedures and the presentation of accounts and discharge are minor. A new provision on the possibility to charge fees by the Agency for capacity building was introduced. The proposal also allows ECHA to maintain a limited fund reserve from income form fees and charges, subject to the specific conditions set out in this proposal.

summary:
PURPOSE: to ensure the alignment of the relevant EU legislation to the amended Common Regulations for the WIPO Lisbon System of Geographical Indications in the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO).
PROPOSED ACT: Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council.
ROLE OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT: the European Parliament decides in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure and on an equal footing with the Council.
BACKGROUND: on 14 July 2025, in the Sixty-Sixth Series of Meetings of the Assemblies of the Member States of WIPO the Assembly of the Lisbon Union adopted the amendments to the Common Regulations under the Lisbon Agreement for the Protection of Appellations of Origin and their International Registration and the Geneva Act of the Lisbon Agreement on Appellations of Origin and Geographical Indications (hereinafter “the Common Regulations”), with 1 July 2026, as their date of entry into force.
The Union is a Contracting Party to the Geneva Act of the Lisbon Agreement on Appellations of Origin and Geographical Indications.
Regulation (EU) 2019/1753 of the European Parliament and of the Council on the action of the Union following its accession to the Geneva Act of the Lisbon Agreement on Appellations of Origin and Geographical Indications establishes the rules and procedures concerning actions of the Union following its accession to the Geneva Act. As a consequence of the adoption of the amendments to the Common Regulations by the Assembly of the Lisbon Union on 14 July 2025, several provisions of Regulation (EU) 2019/1753 will have to be amended by the date of entry into force of the amendments to the Common Regulations to ensure the consistency and coherence of Regulation (EU) 2019/1753 with the updated Common Regulations, and thus to enable the Union to continue to be fully operational as a Contracting Party to the Geneva Act.
CONTENT: as of 1 July 2026, following the new Rule 15 of the Common Regulations, Contracting Parties shall be allowed to submit requests to encode new types of modifications: modification of the name of an Appellation of Origin or Geographical Indication registered under the Geneva Act, modification of the type of good or product and modification of the description of the particulars concerning the quality, reputation or characteristics of the Appellation of Origin or Geographical Indication concerned.
At present, the procedures set out in Regulation (EU) 2019/1753 apply only to the submissions of applications for registration of Appellations of Origin or Geographical Indications of the Union, to the decisions to protect or refuse the protection to the Appellations of Origin or Geographical Indications registered by the other Contracting Parties and to the authorisation to Member States, members of the Lisbon Agreement and joining the Geneva, Act to notify to the International Bureau their Appellations of Origin.
This proposal sets out new procedures in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2019/1753 to:
- facilitate the submission by the Union of modifications to Appellations of Origin or Geographical Indications, of the Union and of its Member States, which are relevant for the protection in the Geneva Act of such Appellations;
- allow the Union to assess whether to protect appellations of origin or geographical indications originating in the territory of contracting parties other than Member States for which a modification has been encoded in the International Register.
These amendments are necessary to allow the Union to meet its obligations under the Geneva Act.
The proposal also provides for administrative simplification by deleting the obligation for Member States which were party of the Lisbon Agreement before the accession of the Union to the Geneva Act to transmit to the Commission any notification made by the International Bureau under the Lisbon Agreement and the obligation for the Commission to transmit those notifications to all other Member States.

text:
2025/0223(COD) | Union Civil Protection Mechanism and Union support for health emergency preparedness and response
Rapporteur: Leire Pajín (S&D) | Lead committee: ENVI

📅 12 November 2026 | ↩️ Plenary sent the file back to committee
What's next: The committee will keep working on the text — typically to continue negotiations — before it returns to plenary. No deadline applies.

Official summary (Legislative Observatory, Legislative proposal published):
PURPOSE: to provide for the Union Civil Protection Mechanism for the period 2028-2034.

PROPOSED ACT: Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council.

ROLE OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT: the European Parliament decides in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure and on an equal footing with the Council.

BACKGROUND: on 16 July 2025, the Commission unveiled its proposal for the next Multiannual Financial Framework 2028-2034 (MFF), a budget of almost EUR 2 trillion between 2028 and 2034 designed to strengthen Europe's sovereignty, competitiveness, and resilience. This proposal is part of a set of sectoral regulations governing programmes under the next MFF.
Given the significant increase in the number and severity of natural and human-induced hazards in recent years, enhanced cooperation in the field of civil protection at Union level is necessary to create a resilient Union with the necessary capacities to anticipate and manage such risks and threats, whatever their nature of origin. The Union Civil Protection Mechanism should fulfil this role by strengthening cooperation and coordination between Member States in order to improve the overall capacity to prevent, prepare for and respond to them.

CONTENT: the proposed regulation provides for the Union Civil Protection Mechanism and sets out Union support for health emergency preparedness and response. It defines the objectives, the budget for the period 2028-2034, the forms of Union financing, and the rules for granting that financing.
General objective
The proposed regulation aims to ensure the protection of people, the environment and property, as well as cultural heritage, against all types of natural and human-induced disasters, including serious cross-border threats to health. It will allow for cross-sectoral coordination in situations where other EU crisis response or risk management mechanisms are applied.
The indicative financial envelope for the implementation of the regulation for the period 2028-2034 is set at EUR 10 675 000 000 in current prices.
The specific objectives pursued are as follows:
- strengthen understanding and anticipation of disaster risks and threats , including those related to climate change and public health, and work proactively to prevent or mitigate their potential impacts, foster prevention and preparedness, and enhance collaboration between civil protection, health and other relevant authorities;
- facilitate capacity building at Union and Member State level, including by encouraging and increasing the uptake and use of research and innovation results in disaster and crisis response, by providing and implementing capacity building programmes such as training and exercises, peer reviews and deployment of experts;
- strengthen preparedness at Member State and Union level, including at all levels of society by: (i) supporting the development of early warning systems to detect and communicate imminent threats of disasters, (ii) promoting the integration of disaster risk reduction and preparedness considerations into policies and financial frameworks at national and Union level, (iii) facilitating preparedness and resilience of all actors and stakeholders, including all levels of government, civil and military authorities, civil society and the private sector;
- facilitate a rapid and effective response within the Union as well as outside the Union, following a request for assistance;
- support the preparedness and response of Member States and the Union to cross-sectoral crises;
- strengthen capacities for prevention, preparedness and rapid response to serious cross-border threats to health and improve the supply of medical countermeasures.
The Commission should work with the High Representative to help develop measures to improve civil-military preparedness and response coordination within the Union, in consultation with Member States.
Emergency Response Coordination Centre
Coordination efforts will be strengthened and further refined through the capacity building of the Emergency Response Coordination Centre (ERCC) and the establishment of a dedicated Crisis Coordination Hub to help Member States anticipate and manage the consequences of crises across all sectors.
The co-financing rates and operational rules established in Decision No 1313/2013 and under the EU4Health programme will be simplified to allow for more efficient and flexible implementation in the event of a fast-evolving crisis.

Source: OEIL procedure file 2025/0223(COD)

text:
2025/0264(CNS) | Association of the overseas countries and territories with the EU including EU/Greenland/Denmark relations
Rapporteur: Barry Andrews (Renew) | Lead committee: DEVE

📅 12 November 2026 | 🗳️ Parliament adopted its opinion (consultation) (460-76, 81 abstentions)
What's next: Now in the Council's hands: it can adopt the act (usually by unanimity), amend it, or park it indefinitely — consultation sets no deadline.

Official summary (Legislative Observatory, Legislative proposal published):
PURPOSE: to amend Decision (EU) 2021/1764 to ensure the continuation of the partnership between the Union and the overseas countries and territories (OCTs) under the 2028-2034 multiannual financial framework (MFF).

PROPOSED ACT: Council Decision.

ROLE OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT: the Council adopts the act after consulting the European Parliament but without being obliged to follow its opinion.

BACKGROUND: this proposal is made in the context of the future multiannual financial framework (MFF) (2028-2034) which has the political ambition of delivering on the Union’s priorities while acting with strength and unity on the global stage over the next decade.
One such priority is stepping up support under the Council Decision on the association of the OCTs with the European Union, including relations between the European Union on one hand, and Greenland and Denmark on the other (Decision on Overseas Association, including Greenland - DOAG), to which the Commission is proposing an amendment.
The 13 OCTs, linked to Denmark, France, and the Netherlands, represent approximately 1 million inhabitants and have the largest EEZ in the world (15 million km²). They are not part of the EU, the single market, or the Schengen area, but their inhabitants are European citizens.
Unlike the NDICI - Global Europe, which establishes a financing instrument (2021-2027), the DOAG is a Council decision that establishes (i) an association of the OCTs with the Union in accordance with the provisions of the Treaty, and (ii) a financing programme for the association. The DOAG does not include a sunset clause linked to the duration of the MFF (with the exception of its financing programme). For this reason, it cannot be merged with Global Europe.
The objectives and mechanisms of the DOAG remain relevant and appropriate. However, given its sunset clause, the financing programme for the association must be resubmitted, including its financial envelope and implementation arrangements.

CONTENT: the proposal seeks to amend Decision (EU) 2021/1764 on the Association of the OCTs with the European Union including relations between the European Union on the one hand, and Greenland and Denmark on the other.
General objective
The general objective of the amending decision is to promote the sustainable economic and social development of the OCTs and to establish close economic relations between them and the Union as a whole.
The association will pursue this general objective by:
- enhancing the OCTs’ competitiveness,
- strengthening the OCTs’ resilience,
- reducing their economic and environmental vulnerability and
- promoting cooperation between them and other partners.
Another aim of this amendment is to preserve the existing ties between the Union on the one hand, and Greenland and Denmark on the other, acknowledging the increased geostrategic position of Greenland in the Arctic, and to preserve existing ties between the Union and the other OCTs, acknowledging their geostrategic positions in the Caribbean, the Indian Ocean, the Atlantic, and the Pacific.
Specific objectives
The specific objectives of this decision are the following:
- to foster and support cooperation with OCTs , including in addressing their major challenges and reaching the sustainable development goals;
- to support and to cooperate with Greenland in addressing its major challenges , notably by raising the education level and strengthening the capacity of its public administration to formulate and implement national policies; and
- to support the sustainable development of strategic sectors - including critical raw materials, renewable energy, secured and trusted digital connectivity, and sustainable tourism - within the framework of a strengthened partnership between the EU and Greenland.
Boosting the strategic investment agenda under the Global Gateway
To bring the EU-OCTs partnership more in line with the commitments under the Global Gateway strategy, it is proposed to merge allocations for territorial (bilateral) and regional cooperation for OCTs, and prepare a separate financing envelope for Greenland, dividing financing between cooperation with the OCTs other than Greenland, and cooperation with Greenland, while providing for flexible implementation modalities.
Reinforcing coherence with the broader EU financing architecture
It is proposed to further reinforce the ‘external’ DOAG dimension specifying the eligibility and access of the OCTs to relevant Union programmes and external financing instruments by consistently applying related cross-references/mirror clauses across all relevant basic acts. The objective is to increase the complementarities of EU actions and strengthen the integration of the OCTs into the EU’s competitiveness agenda.
Strengthening focus and improving the structure of the dialogue with the OCTs
- An ‘OCTs-EU Forum’ will meet every two years to bring together the OCTs’ authorities, representatives of the Member States and the Commission. Members of the European Parliament, representatives of the EIB and representatives of the outermost regions will, where appropriate, be associated with the OCTs-EU Forum.
- Trilateral consultations between the Commission, the OCTs and the Member States to which they are linked will be organised at least three times a year on the initiative of the Commission or at the request of OCTs and of the Member States to which they are linked.
Multiannual indicative programmes, action plans and measures
The Commission will adopt, pursuant to this Decision, multiannual indicative programmes. Programming documents, action plans and measures will be adopted by means of implementing acts, with the exception of action plans and individual measures for which Union financing does not exceed EUR 2 million and special and support measures for which Union financing does not exceed EUR 5 million.
Budgetary implications
The European Commission proposes to allocate an indicative financial envelope of EUR 999 million (in current prices) to the association’s funding programme for 2028-2034.

Official summary (Legislative Observatory, Legislative proposal published):
PURPOSE: to provide for the Union Civil Protection Mechanism for the period 2028-2034.

PROPOSED ACT: Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council.

ROLE OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT: the European Parliament decides in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure and on an equal footing with the Council.

BACKGROUND: on 16 July 2025, the Commission unveiled its proposal for the next Multiannual Financial Framework 2028-2034 (MFF), a budget of almost EUR 2 trillion between 2028 and 2034 designed to strengthen Europe's sovereignty, competitiveness, and resilience. This proposal is part of a set of sectoral regulations governing programmes under the next MFF.
Given the significant increase in the number and severity of natural and human-induced hazards in recent years, enhanced cooperation in the field of civil protection at Union level is necessary to create a resilient Union with the necessary capacities to anticipate and manage such risks and threats, whatever their nature of origin. The Union Civil Protection Mechanism should fulfil this role by strengthening cooperation and coordination between Member States in order to improve the overall capacity to prevent, prepare for and respond to them.

CONTENT: the proposed regulation provides for the Union Civil Protection Mechanism and sets out Union support for health emergency preparedness and response. It defines the objectives, the budget for the period 2028-2034, the forms of Union financing, and the rules for granting that financing.
General objective
The proposed regulation aims to ensure the protection of people, the environment and property, as well as cultural heritage, against all types of natural and human-induced disasters, including serious cross-border threats to health. It will allow for cross-sectoral coordination in situations where other EU crisis response or risk management mechanisms are applied.
The indicative financial envelope for the implementation of the regulation for the period 2028-2034 is set at EUR 10 675 000 000 in current prices.
The specific objectives pursued are as follows:
- strengthen understanding and anticipation of disaster risks and threats , including those related to climate change and public health, and work proactively to prevent or mitigate their potential impacts, foster prevention and preparedness, and enhance collaboration between civil protection, health and other relevant authorities;
- facilitate capacity building at Union and Member State level, including by encouraging and increasing the uptake and use of research and innovation results in disaster and crisis response, by providing and implementing capacity building programmes such as training and exercises, peer reviews and deployment of experts;
- strengthen preparedness at Member State and Union level, including at all levels of society by: (i) supporting the development of early warning systems to detect and communicate imminent threats of disasters, (ii) promoting the integration of disaster risk reduction and preparedness considerations into policies and financial frameworks at national and Union level, (iii) facilitating preparedness and resilience of all actors and stakeholders, including all levels of government, civil and military authorities, civil society and the private sector;
- facilitate a rapid and effective response within the Union as well as outside the Union, following a request for assistance;
- support the preparedness and response of Member States and the Union to cross-sectoral crises;
- strengthen capacities for prevention, preparedness and rapid response to serious cross-border threats to health and improve the supply of medical countermeasures.
The Commission should work with the High Representative to help develop measures to improve civil-military preparedness and response coordination within the Union, in consultation with Member States.

Coordination efforts will be strengthened and further refined through the capacity building of the Emergency Response Coordination Centre (ERCC) and the establishment of a dedicated Crisis Coordination Hub to help Member States anticipate and manage the consequences of crises across all sectors.

This proposal would amend an existing EU decision so that the partnership between the EU and the overseas countries and territories (OCTs) can continue under the EU's next long-term budget, covering 2028 to 2034. The Council would adopt the measure after consulting the European Parliament, but would not have to follow Parliament's opinion.

The reason for the change is that the current decision has a sunset clause tied to the budget period, so its funding programme has to be submitted again, including its financial amount and how it will be carried out. The 13 OCTs, linked to Denmark, France and the Netherlands, have about 1 million inhabitants and the largest exclusive economic zone in the world. They are not part of the EU, the single market or the Schengen area, but their inhabitants are European citizens. The decision also covers relations with Greenland and Denmark, reflecting Greenland's growing strategic importance in the Arctic.

The overall aim is to promote sustainable economic and social development in the OCTs and to build close economic ties between them and the EU. The partnership would work toward this by improving the OCTs' competitiveness and resilience, reducing their economic and environmental vulnerability, and encouraging cooperation with other partners. It also has specific goals: supporting cooperation with the OCTs on their major challenges and the UN sustainable development goals, helping Greenland raise education levels and strengthen its public administration, and supporting sustainable development in strategic sectors such as critical raw materials, renewable energy, secure digital connectivity and sustainable tourism.

Several changes are proposed to make the partnership work better. Territorial and regional funding for the OCTs would be combined, with a separate funding share for Greenland, and implementation would allow flexibility. The OCTs would be given clearer access to relevant EU programmes and external financing tools, to tie them more closely to the EU's competitiveness goals. A dialogue structure would also be set up: an OCTs-EU Forum meeting every two years, with OCT authorities, Member State representatives and the Commission, and possibly Members of the European Parliament, the European Investment Bank and representatives of the outermost regions. Trilateral consultations between the Commission, the OCTs and their linked Member States would be held at least three times a year.

This proposal would update the EU rules on key information documents (KIDs), the short plain-language documents that explain the features, risks and costs of packaged retail and insurance-based investment products (PRIIPs). These products are often offered by banks to ordinary savers, for example to save for a house or a child's education, but they can be complicated and hard to compare. The existing rules, set out in Regulation (EU) No 1286/2014, require producers and sellers to give investors these documents. The proposal keeps the main framework but makes targeted changes to it. The European Parliament and the Council would decide on it together, on an equal footing.

The main changes update the legal references to the prospectus rules, so the right securities are covered. They also remove retail products that provide immediate annuities with no redemption phase from the scope of the rules. For products that offer several investment options, the proposal sets out the conditions for presenting costs clearly, so investors can compare the choices.

The documents would also change in content. A new "Product at a glance" section would summarise the type of product, its costs, its level of risk, its recommended holding period and whether it includes an insurance benefit. The "comprehension alert," which warns about especially complex products, would be removed because it had not worked well and could discourage people from buying simpler products. A new section titled "How environmentally sustainable is this product?" would give investors a standard set of information on the sustainability of relevant products.

Finally, the proposal modernises how the documents are delivered. Electronic delivery would be preferred, but clients could request a paper copy free of charge. The European Supervisory Authorities would be asked to draft technical standards on how the information is presented, including features that make it accessible to visually impaired readers.

The European Parliament has adopted a set of changes to a proposed EU directive that would simplify the rules for the Infrastructure for Spatial Information in the Union, known as INSPIRE. The vote was 515 in favour, 108 against, with 35 abstentions. The changes were sent to the committee responsible for negotiations with the other EU institutions.

The proposal is part of a wider EU effort to simplify environmental rules and to support the GreenData4All initiative. It would remove some technical requirements for network services and data sharing from the INSPIRE Directive, relying instead on general EU data legislation.

Parliament broadly supports the goal of simplifying the rules and making them consistent with general data law. However, it is concerned that some of the Commission's approach could weaken protections that are specific to environmental geographic data.

Parliament's main amendments stress that good environmental data is essential for making, carrying out, monitoring and enforcing EU environmental laws. Member States would need to make sure that spatial datasets and services are provided using open, documented, vendor-neutral standards, including those of the International Organization for Standardization and the Open Geospatial Consortium, and that the technical choices made do not stop data from being found, accessed, used and reused across borders.

On the network of services, Member States would have to make relevant spatial datasets available and accessible under the EU open data directive, in a way that supports discovery, access and comparability across the EU. Public authorities would have to be able to link their datasets to relevant data-sharing services, and third parties whose datasets meet the required metadata and interoperability rules could request the same option.

On data sharing, Member States would have to ensure that public authorities can access and exchange the spatial data they need to carry out public tasks affecting the environment. Where necessary, countries would adopt or keep national measures to make this access effective.

The European Parliament has voted on a proposed temporary rule that would let online messaging and communication providers use certain technologies to scan personal and other data in order to detect and fight online child sexual abuse. The rule would temporarily set aside some privacy requirements from an existing EU directive on electronic communications, and it applies to services that are not based on phone numbers.

Parliament proposed changes to the Council's version of the rule. Its main change would exclude from the rule any communications that use, have used, or will use end-to-end encryption, meaning messages that only the people communicating can read.

In the first vote, a simple majority voted against the Council's position, with 314 in favour of rejecting it, 276 against, and 17 abstentions. A second vote on rejecting Parliament's amended position did not get a majority, with 276 in favour, 286 against, and 30 abstentions. Because neither side won a majority in that second vote, the second reading has ended.

This measure sets out the rules for how the European Union handles the leftover money and assets of the European Coal and Steel Community, which expired in July 2002. Under an existing protocol, those assets are used to fund research in the coal and steel sectors through the Research Fund for Coal and Steel. The measure would be adopted as a Council Decision, and the Council can only adopt it if the European Parliament has given its consent.

The European Commission would be responsible for managing the assets and for putting in place the measures needed to carry out the protocol. The aim is to keep an annual research allocation of up to EUR 120 million for each year from 2027 to 2033. The reason for this is that the income from the assets has been falling, and in 2024 and 2025 the calls for research were paid for entirely by selling assets. From August 2027, the old Community is expected to have no remaining debts or claims, which would allow it to be wound up and make it possible to sell part of the assets.

Any assets left over after that period would form a final allocation for 2034, set at their market value when transferred to the fund, taking market conditions into account. That money would then go toward coal and steel research in 2034 and later years. The annual funding would come from investment income and cash raised by selling some assets, and it would be treated as earmarked revenue in the EU budget.

The research money would be split through work programmes, with 27.2% going to coal-related research and 72.8% to steel-related research. The steel research would focus on cleaner, low-carbon production, stronger steel products, resource conservation, recycling, skills, working conditions and digital technology. The coal research would focus on managing a fair transition, including reusing old or closing coal mines and their infrastructure and the regions around them. The Commission would be allowed to change the 27.2% and 72.8% split through delegated acts if needed to make full use of the assets in 2034.

Rapporteur: Kamila Gasiuk-Pihowicz (EPP) | Lead committee: ITRE

What's next: Trilogue talks with the Council can begin once the Council side has its own mandate. Closed-door rounds follow; timing is not published.

Official summary (Legislative Observatory, Legislative proposal published):
PURPOSE: to establish the Connecting Europe Facility for the period 2028-2034.

PROPOSED ACT: Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council.

ROLE OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT: the European Parliament decides in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure and on an equal footing with the Council.

BACKGROUND: on 16 July 2025, the European Commission unveiled its proposal for the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) 2028-2034 , a EUR 2 trillion budget designed to strengthen Europe's sovereignty, competitiveness, and resilience. This new MFF will significantly enhance the EU's capacity to deliver on core policies while addressing new and emerging priorities.
Based on the positive experience from the implementation of the previous Connecting Europe Facility (CEF) programmes, the Commission proposes to continue the implementation of the new programme, for both transport and energy, with direct management by the Commission and an executive agency.
This proposal aims to set the legal basis for CEF for the period 2028-2034.

CONTENT: the proposed regulation establishes the Connecting Europe Facility and lays down the objectives of the Programme, its budget for the period 2028-2034, the forms of Union funding and the rules for providing such funding.
A financial envelope of EUR 81.4 billion is included under this new framework for the Connecting Europe Facility for investments in trans-European networks for transport and energy infrastructure, including military mobility and renewable energy projects.
The distribution of the amount will be as follows:
- EUR 51.5 billion for the specific objectives on transport and military mobility ;
- EUR 29.9 billion for the specific objectives on energy .
General objectives
The general objectives of the programme are to build, develop, secure, modernise and complete the trans-European networks in the transport and energy sectors, facilitate military mobility on the trans-European transport networks, facilitate cross-border cooperation in the field of renewable energy, and facilitate the synergies among the transport and energy sectors.
In the transport sector , CEF contributes to the completion of core network of the trans-European transport network (TEN-T) by 2030 and the extended core network by 2040 through building and upgrading infrastructure that is required for seamless cross-border transport operations. This will lead to a high-performing network for passengers and goods transportation. CEF also supports the adaptation of relevant parts of the TEN-T network to military mobility requirements.
In the field of military mobility , the Programme aims to contribute to enabling transportation of military equipment and personnel across the EU at speed and scale, taking into account the military expertise at EU level.
In the energy sector , CEF contributes to the development of projects of common interest and projects of mutual interest, with a view to promoting the completion of the Energy Union, the integration of an efficient and competitive internal energy market and the interoperability of networks across borders and sectors, to facilitating decarbonisation of the economy, to promoting energy efficiency and to ensuring security of supply.
Furthermore, CEF facilitates cross-border cooperation in the field of renewable energy, through cross-border renewable energy projects or competitive bidding for new renewable energy projects under the Union renewable energy financing mechanism.
The programme should be operational with the start of the next MFF beginning of 2028.

Source: OEIL procedure file 2025/0221(COD)

Based on the positive experience from the implementation of the previous Connecting Europe Facility (CEF) programmes, the Commission proposes to continue the implementation of the new programme, for both transport and energy, with direct management by the Commission and an executive agency.
This proposal aims to set the legal basis for CEF for the period 2028-2034.

CONTENT: the proposed regulation establishes the Connecting Europe Facility and lays down the objectives of the Programme, its budget for the period 2028-2034, the forms of Union funding and the rules for providing such funding.
A financial envelope of EUR 81.4 billion is included under this new framework for the Connecting Europe Facility for investments in trans-European networks for transport and energy infrastructure, including military mobility and renewable energy projects.
The distribution of the amount will be as follows:
- EUR 51.5 billion for the specific objectives on transport and military mobility ;
- EUR 29.9 billion for the specific objectives on energy .
General objectives
The general objectives of the programme are to build, develop, secure, modernise and complete the trans-European networks in the transport and energy sectors, facilitate military mobility on the trans-European transport networks, facilitate cross-border cooperation in the field of renewable energy, and facilitate the synergies among the transport and energy sectors.
In the transport sector , CEF contributes to the completion of core network of the trans-European transport network (TEN-T) by 2030 and the extended core network by 2040 through building and upgrading infrastructure that is required for seamless cross-border transport operations. This will lead to a high-performing network for passengers and goods transportation. CEF also supports the adaptation of relevant parts of the TEN-T network to military mobility requirements.
In the field of military mobility , the Programme aims to contribute to enabling transportation of military equipment and personnel across the EU at speed and scale, taking into account the military expertise at EU level.
In the energy sector , CEF contributes to the development of projects of common interest and projects of mutual interest, with a view to promoting the completion of the Energy Union, the integration of an efficient and competitive internal energy market and the interoperability of networks across borders and sectors, to facilitating decarbonisation of the economy, to promoting energy efficiency and to ensuring security of supply.
Furthermore, CEF facilitates cross-border cooperation in the field of renewable energy, through cross-border renewable energy projects or competitive bidding for new renewable energy projects under the Union renewable energy financing mechanism.
The programme should be operational with the start of the next MFF beginning of 2028.
