ai_summary:
The European Parliament approved a proposed regulation on the European Chemicals Agency by 561 votes to 13, with 39 abstentions. The measure sets out the Agency's job: helping to carry out EU rules on the dangers, risks, safe use and environmental sustainability of chemicals, giving independent scientific advice, watching for new chemical risks, and gathering and sharing information. Its main aims are to protect human health and the environment, including vulnerable groups, while helping chemicals move freely within the EU single market. It also aims for consistent chemical assessment across the EU, taking account of the needs of micro, small and medium-sized businesses, and it should promote replacing hazardous chemicals and developing non-animal testing methods. The Agency must also manage conflicts of interest and run yearly training for staff and committee members.

The Management Board would include one representative from each Member State, six people appointed by the Commission (three Commission representatives and three representing interested parties), and two independent people appointed by the European Parliament. Committees would support cooperation with other countries and international bodies on chemical safety, including technical help for developing countries.

Within its adopted budget, the Agency would decide how to spread its money across its work and report annually to Parliament and the Council. Two years after the regulation applies, and every five years after that, the Commission would review how the reserve works and whether the fees paid to the Agency are adequate. The Agency would also help Member States and the Commission with research and innovation, including supporting safer alternatives to hazardous chemicals and non-animal testing methods.

The Parliament or a Member State could ask the Agency for scientific advice, after consulting the Commission. The Agency may refuse requests that are redundant, outside its remit, compromise its missions, or rest on insufficient information, and it must publish its reasons. It would set response deadlines, which can be extended with justification. Finally, the Agency would work with other EU bodies, such as the health, environment, food safety, medicines and workplace safety agencies, to share data and methods, develop chemical assessments without animal testing, and promote the "One Health" approach.

The vote was 311 in favour and 261 against, with 38 abstentions. The change aims to keep this document short and easy to read by cutting out anything that is not essential or is repeated.

Under the change, the document must stand on its own and be clearly separate from marketing material. It should not point to marketing material or contain investment recommendations. It may refer to other documents, such as a prospectus where relevant, but only for information that belongs in the key information document itself. If a product offers a range of investment options that cannot fit in one short document, the document should still give at least a general description of those options and the product's costs apart from the costs of the investment options.

Product makers must give investors tools that help them research and compare the different investment options. Where technically possible, these tools should show the total cost of the product, including the cost of the insurance cover, as well as risks and performance, and they should link to the detailed pre-contract information for the underlying investments. Investors must also be told the total cost before they are bound by any contract or offer, and this is also met if the information is provided electronically.

The electronic and paper versions must have identical content. Consumers can ask for a paper copy, which must be provided free of charge. The European supervisory authorities must make the document streamlined, standardised and user-friendly, with simple cost information, and where useful, tables and graphs. The information must be limited to what is strictly necessary, and performance information must be comparable across different types of products.

The document will also include the sustainability profile of these products, since investors increasingly want that information. By 31 December 2030, the Commission must report on whether an EU-wide comparison tool for these products is feasible, assessing its impact, costs and benefits. If appropriate, the report will be accompanied by a legislative proposal.
